sections.h2: Which Chatham County office does what on property tax?
sections.html:
Chatham County splits the work between a Listing Division, an Appraisal Division and a Collections Division, all under Tax Administration. The Listing Division sits at 12 East Street in Pittsboro, ground floor of the government annex facing the Pittsboro traffic circle, and its public counter operates on weekdays, eight to five. Correspondence goes to PO Box 908 in Pittsboro (ZIP 27312), and the listing line is 919-542-8250.

Questions about what your house is worth on the tax roll go to the Appraisal Division at 919-542-8211. The county states the mission as fair, accurate valuation of real and personal property across Chatham. Bills, payments and returned-check issues go through Collections.

Census QuickFacts counts 85,111 people in Chatham for mid-2025, 11.6% more than in 2020, spread over 681.68 land square miles: see Census QuickFacts. Pittsboro, Siler City and Goldston levy their own town taxes, and slices of Chatham near Cary and Apex are billed for those towns too. That mix is why two Chatham neighbors can have different bills on similar houses.

sections.h2: How often does Chatham County reappraise real estate?
sections.html:
Chatham reappraises every four years, which is tighter than the eight-year ceiling North Carolina sets for every county under G.S. 105-286. The most recent reappraisal took effect on January 1, 2025, and the one before it was in 2021. If the county keeps that rhythm, the next value date lands in 2029, though the Appraisal Division is the office to confirm that with.

For the 2025 round, county appraisers studied recorded sales, building cost data and income and expense figures from commercial property to estimate values for more than 48,000 parcels. Notices went out by mail in March 2025. Many parts of the county went up in value from 2021, a few went down and some stayed about the same.

The tax rate is a separate step. The county explained then that bills stay unknowable until each taxing body adopts a rate from its budget. In the budget approved for fiscal year 2026-27, commissioners kept the county rate at 60 cents per $100 of valuation after the revaluation year, as the county's budget announcement put it.

sections.h2: What are the 2026 property tax rates in Chatham County?
sections.html:
The county-only rate is 0.60, and every other district adds its own piece on top, according to the county's 2026 rate sheet. The sheet prints a district rate and a combined rate for each area, so the combined figure is the one that matches a bill. A few lines from that sheet are below.

The county budget year begins July 1, which is also when commissioners and the towns fix rates. A call to the tax office will tell you which district covers a given street address.

sections.h2: What is the path for contesting a Chatham County value?
sections.html:
Begin with the county's comparison tool, file with the Appraisal Division next, and take the matter to the county's equalization board only if the staff review leaves you unsatisfied. During the 2025 reappraisal the county urged owners to test their notice against nearby sales on its Comper website. An online appeal form lives on the appraisal page, and a printable paper form is available too.

  • Comparable sales, from your own research, the county's site or a real estate professional.
  • Photos of the inside and outside of the property, showing condition and upgrades.
  • A recent fee appraisal, such as one done for a purchase or refinance.

After an appeal is received, a tax office representative contacts the owner to go over the value. Still unresolved? Request a hearing, and the board mails its written finding. The 2025 appeal window shut on May 19, 2025 at five in the afternoon. For 2026 the board began April 6 and adjourned April 20, and it took no new appeals after adjourning.

Two statutes set the outer frame. G.S. 105-322 puts the board's first sitting in April or early May, and G.S. 105-290 gives a 30-day clock for taking a loss to the Property Tax Commission.

sections.h2: Which Chatham County relief programs reduce a tax bill?
sections.html:
Chatham runs three state programs plus one local grant. The state-program applications must reach the Tax Listing Office before June 1 of the year you qualify, and the county page lists the following.

  • Elderly or disabled exclusion: $25,000 or half the residence's appraised value, whichever is larger, for residents of 65 or more, or with a total and permanent disability, whose income does not exceed $38,800.
  • Disabled veteran exclusion: $45,000 off the appraised value, for a resident who is a disabled veteran or an unmarried surviving spouse; the NCDVA-9 form comes from the NC Division of Veterans Affairs.
  • Circuit breaker deferment: taxes capped at a share of income for 65-plus or totally disabled owners with income at or under $58,200 and five calendar years of owning and living in the house. Excess tax stays as a lien, and the latest three years of deferred tax come due with interest on a disqualifying event. A new application is needed each year.
  • Low Income Tax Relief Program: up to $500, never more than 50% of the current bill, for residents with five years of ownership and residence in the home and household income at or below 60% of area median income. Households receiving Food and Nutrition Services skip the income paperwork.

Disability claims require a certificate from a North Carolina physician or a government agency. Heirs or executors must tell the office when a recipient dies, and a surviving spouse reapplies for the following year. Failing to report a disqualifying event means recovery of the exclusion plus penalties and interest.

sections.h2: What are the due dates, and what if tax is still owed at closing?
sections.html:
Payment is due each September 1 and carries no interest through January 5, under G.S. 105-360. Interest of 2% begins January 6, and from February 1 it adds three-fourths of one percent for every month or fraction. A check or electronic payment that bounces draws a penalty of $25 or 10% of the payment, whichever is greater, up to $1,000, according to the Collections Division page.

A tax lien attaches on the listing date under G.S. 105-355, so the bill follows the house, not the seller. The closing office normally settles the current year's tax out of the seller's money, and the buyer carries it forward. Owners who let a bill go unpaid can face a tax foreclosure sale held at the courthouse door, with the sale price applied to taxes, penalties, interest and costs under G.S. 105-374.

For 2020 to 2024 Census data shows 80.6% owner-occupancy, a $446,200 median home value and $94,317 in median household income. Seniors make up 28.0% of the county, the group the exclusion and deferment programs are built for. Anyone receiving a program benefit should ask the Listing Division what a sale does to it.

sections.h2: What does recording a Chatham County deed cost?
sections.html:
North Carolina's excise tax of $1.00 per $500 of consideration is the seller's to pay at the register of deeds office, per G.S. 105-228.30. The Chatham County Register of Deeds charges $26.00 to record a deed of up to 15 pages and $4.00 for each additional page. A deed of trust runs $64 for up to 35 pages.

These recording amounts mirror the uniform schedule in G.S. 161-10. Your closing office will supply exact settlement figures, because they turn on the price and the number of pages.

faqs.q: Where do I pay or question my Chatham County property tax bill?
faqs.a: Call the Tax Administration offices in Pittsboro. The Listing Division answers at 919-542-8250 and the Appraisal Division at 919-542-8211. Collections handles payments, and the Listing Division is at 12 East Street, open 8:00 to 5:00 on weekdays.

faqs.q: What is the Chatham County county-only tax rate?
faqs.a: The county-only rate on the 2026 rate sheet is 0.60, matching the 60 cents per $100 of valuation the commissioners kept for fiscal year 2026-27. Town and fire districts add their own rates, so the full rate turns on the parcel's location.

faqs.q: Is the 2026 appeal window still open?
faqs.a: No. The Board of Equalization and Review adjourned on April 20, 2026 at 5:00 p.m. and accepted no more appeals for tax year 2026. Owners can still talk to the Appraisal Division about errors, and the next reappraisal cycle brings a new notice and a new window.

faqs.q: Can a Chatham County senior get a lower assessment?
faqs.a: Yes, if income and age fit. The elderly or disabled exclusion removes the greater of $25,000 or 50% of a home's appraised value for owners 65 or older with income up to $38,800. File with the Tax Listing Office before June 1.

faqs.q: Who pays the deed excise tax in Chatham County?
faqs.a: The seller does. The statute puts the $1.00 per $500 charge on the transferor, payable to the register of deeds ahead of recording, and the closing office usually takes it from proceeds.
